newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US sees cyberspace copyright treaties passed.
newsitem.headline: US sees cyberspace copyright treaties passed.

text.p: Nearly three weeks of global talks to revise copyright rules for cyberspace were bogged down in disputes Thursday, but a senior U.S. official said he was optimistic that a deal would be reached by a Friday deadline.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of Commerce Bruce Lehman said delegates from 160 nations were working on a number of compromise solutions and were likely to complete their talks and adopt the treaties Friday.
"Getting a consensus among all the countries is the issue. Different countries have had different versions and that's the problem," Lehman said in an interview.
"But we're on the threshold of success. I think we're going to come to a solution to the problem. There are alternatives on the table."

More than 800 delegates have been locked in a gloomy Geneva conference centre since Dec. 2 debating three treaties -- on literary and artistic works, on rights of performers and producers of music and on database producers.

The talks aim to upgrade the century-old Berne convention on copyrights to cover the borderless world of the Internet, which has ripped up the rule books because computer users can copy and distribute anything from music to software at the click of a mouse.
The biggest dispute, over exemptions from copyright rules in the digital era, pits music, software, entertainment and other copyright-based industries against the Internet and online service giants.
Online and Internet companies are furious that the treaties make even innocent Web surfing -- which by definition requires that a computer make transient copies -- a copyright violation.
They say this would expose them to multibillion-dollar liability for copyright violations between millions of service users and give sweeping powers to copyright-based industries.
Unless the treaties spell out legal protection for them, they want the contentious parts deleted altogether.
Lehman said deletion was one issue under discussion along with other compromise solutions but gave no details.
Telecommunications giants such as Bell Atlantic Corp., America Online Inc. and Nynex Corp. say they cannot police treaties that apply copyright rules to both permanent and temporary reproductions.

Online companies allege that music and record companies want to use the Internet as a cash cow, leaving what they say is the impossible task of policing copyright violations under the proposed treaties to the Internet community.
Lehman, seeking to reassure online companies, said he could swear they had nothing to fear in the draft treaties.

"I said many many times and I'll say it again and I'm prepared to testify under oath before the U.S. Senate that nothing in these treaties in themselves make anything a violation of the U.S. law that's not already a violation of the U.S. law," he said.

"We're looking for something that would provide for effective protection for authors' rights in the new digital environment and at the same time meet the legitimate concerns of the vast majority of national delegations," he added.
